name: Dervish Board
description: An electric skateboard with hub motors in the rear wheels, common among Tier 1-2 youth. Factory models exist but most Dervishes are hand-built from scavenged parts — a plank of carbon fiber or even wood, truck-mounted motors from dead appliances, and a battery taped to the underside. They're fast, terrifying, and the preferred transport of couriers who know the streets well enough to ride at 40 km/h through crowds.
propulsion: Electric hub motors, DIY battery packs
autonomy: Manual only. Gyro-assist on factory models.
armament: None. But they make excellent improvised weapons.
common_usage: Youth transport, courier work, street racing. A rite of passage in The Shelf.
story_hooks: A courier's Dervish board has a scavenged chip that gives it unexpected capabilities — it adjusts balance before the rider reacts
Underground Dervish races through the L-train support columns are a major betting scene
physical_description: A stripped-down electric skateboard with a warped plank of carbon fiber or weathered wood bolted to mismatched aluminum trucks, the undercarriage a tangle of exposed wiring and a bulky battery pack held down with automotive tape and zip-ties. The hub motors in the rear wheels are salvaged from dead appliances—dented, repaired with epoxy, their casings scrawled with gang tags or worn smooth by countless hands. Most Dervishes bear the scars of hard riding: cracked grip tape, chipped edges, burn marks from friction, and the acrid smell of overworked electronics.
